what_it_does: Modern servers receive network packets at ever-increasing speeds, and a burst of incoming traffic can pile up unevenly across the CPU cores meant to handle it, causing some cores to queue up badly while others sit idle — raising response latency. Intel's DLB (Dynamic Load Balancer) is a hardware chip that distributes this incoming work across cores, but the host CPU still has to do significant work just to prepare and hand each packet's work description to the DLB. This paper first benchmarks DLB against software-only load balancers to understand the bottlenecks, then proposes AccDirect: a design where the network card (NIC) bypasses the CPU entirely by using PCIe Peer-to-Peer communication — a direct data path between two chips on the same PCIe bus — to write work descriptions straight into the DLB's queues. Removing the CPU from this hot path eliminates the wasted host CPU cycles that were the remaining overhead.
